pr.title: match lowering: eagerly simplify match pairs
pr.description:
This removes one important complication from match lowering. Before this, match pair simplification (which includes collecting bindings and type ascriptions) was intertwined with the whole match lowering algorithm.

I'm avoiding this by storing in each `MatchPair` the sub-`MatchPair`s that correspond to its subfields. This makes it possible to simplify everything (except or-patterns) in `Candidate::new()`.

This should open up further simplifications. It will also give us proper control over the order of bindings.

r? @matthewjasper
pr.author: Nadrieril

processing.reason: PR 120904 ("match lowering: eagerly simplify match pairs") is a structural/semantics-preserving refactor, not a wrong-output bug fix. The old code simplified MatchPairs lazily inside the main lowering loop and recomputed subpairs at test time; the new code precomputes and simplifies each MatchPair's subpairs in Candidate::new/MatchPair::new and expands cached subpairs after a successful test. The PR's own evidence and the supplied MIR diff show only basic-block/order changes: in exponential_or.match_tuple the same switchInt tests on the Option discriminant, the Some payload, and _1.0 are merely reordered, with identical targets/edges. The added invariant assertions and the `fully_matched` explicit-assignment cleanup guard against future mistakes; they do not describe a confirmed value-level miscompilation. The intermediate patch series is corrected within the same PR before merge, and no historical code presented here drops, duplicates, or misroutes a binding/ascription in a way observable in source semantics. Therefore any concrete original-vs-transformed function pair that produced different numeric/boolean/character results would have to invent an unrelated rewrite (e.g., deliberately skipping or duplicating a subpair expansion), which the task forbids. There is no source-grounded historical wrong transformation to validate as a semantic counterexample.

analysis.summary: Match lowering was refactored to eagerly compute each MatchPair's recursive subpairs when the candidate is created, simplify those subpairs once, and later expand a fully matched test pair into its precomputed subpairs. This removes the historical intertwining of binding/ascription collection with the main lowering algorithm and avoids repeatedly attempting to simplify pairs that cannot be simplified. The SimplifyCfg-initial MIR expectation change in exponential_or is an order-only change in the emitted switch/discriminant tests, not evidence that SimplifyCfg itself rewrote values incorrectly.
analysis.originalLogic: Before this PR, Candidate::new created a single MatchPair and the main lowering loop called simplify_candidate/simplify_match_pairs. Each successful simplification pushed new match pairs and bindings/ascriptions into the candidate; the loop continued until a fixed point, re-processing unsimplifiable pairs on each iteration. When a test fully matched a variant, constant, or slice pattern, helper functions such as candidate_after_variant_switch, candidate_after_slice_test, and candidate_without_match_pair removed the tested MatchPair and recomputed/expanded its subpairs at test time.
analysis.incorrectTransformation: The historical implementation did not cache subpairs in MatchPair. It left the tested pair in place and expanded it only after the test succeeded, recomputing field/slice/downcast places then. It also repeatedly re-entered simplify_match_pair for pairs that had already been found unsimplifiable. The refactor instead computes subpairs once in MatchPair::new/Candidate::new, simplifies them once, and replaces a fully matched pair with its stored subpairs. This is an optimization/structural cleanup, not a confirmed wrong-output bug fix.
analysis.inputDomain: Rust source match expressions lowered by rustc_mir_build whose patterns contain nested constructors, tuple/struct fields, enum variants, slices/arrays, derefs, bindings (`x @ P`), type ascriptions, constants, ranges, and or-patterns, especially combinations where a refutable test fully determines a variant, constant, length, or range.
analysis.trigger: A candidate is created from a pattern with nested subpatterns, so its MatchPairs can be simplified eagerly; later a test fully matches one of those MatchPairs and must be replaced by its cached subpairs. The exponential_or `match_tuple` test also shows that eager simplification changes the order in which switch/discriminant tests appear in MIR.
preconditions: Each MatchPair's subpairs are precomputed and recursively simplified before test lowering uses the pair.
A MatchPair is simplified exactly once; simplification has side effects on bindings and ascriptions.
All MatchPairs in a candidate are recursively simplified, and or-patterns are sorted to the end.
Test merging explicitly records whether the test fully matched the pair before replacing it with its subpairs.
pitfalls: Re-simplifying a MatchPair can duplicate bindings or type ascriptions because simplification mutates binding/ascription vectors; the patch temporarily asserted `assert!(match_pair.subpairs.is_empty(), "mustn't simplify a match pair twice");`.
Do not default `fully_matched` to false implicitly in every test arm; the PR explicitly changed this because a missing assignment could silently skip replacing a matched pair with its subpairs.
Or-patterns are excluded from eager simplification and must remain sorted after match pairs for the single-or-candidate switch optimization.

The changed exponential_or expectation is order-only: `switchInt((_1.0: u32))` moves from bb0 to bb3 while the Option discriminant test moves to bb0; do not attribute this block reordering to a wrong SimplifyCfg rewrite.
The MatchPair invariants state bindings and ascriptions are not mutated outside Candidate::new(), so later test lowering must expand cached subpairs rather than rebuilding them.
analysis.testStrategy: Use a mir-opt test such as tests/mir-opt/exponential_or.rs revision `match_tuple`, with a tuple containing an Option and or-patterns. Compare MIR after SimplifyCfg-initial and check that toggling eager MatchPair simplification preserves the same switch/discriminant tests and edges, allowing basic-block order to differ. Add focused source cases with nested bindings and type ascriptions inside variants and or-patterns to verify each binding/ascription is produced once, and cases where a test fully matches a variant or slice to verify the pair is replaced by its subpairs. No compiler execution was performed here.
evidence: match lowering: eagerly simplify match pairs

This removes one important complication from match lowering. Before this, match pair simplification (which includes collecting bindings and type ascriptions) was intertwined with the whole match lowering algorithm.
This makes it possible to simplify everything (except or-patterns) in `Candidate::new()`.
Don't repeatedly simplify already-simplified match pairs
// Invariant: all the `MatchPair`s are recursively simplified.
// Invariant: or-patterns must be sorted at the end.
assert!(match_pair.subpairs.is_empty(), "mustn't simplify a match pair twice");
Don't default `fully_matched` to false to avoid mistakes
// Replace the match pair by its sub-pairs.
switchInt((_1.0: u32)) -> [1: bb2, 4: bb2, otherwise: bb1];
